summary: Describes the SASLprep profile of stringprep, for preparing Unicode user names and passwords for comparison, intended for use with SASL. It was replaced by RFC 7613.

plainLanguage.summary: SASLprep rewrites a user name or password into one standard form before a server compares it with a stored value. It removes differences that come from how the characters were typed, and it refuses inputs that are not plain text. It is meant for simple user names and passwords, not for email addresses or domain names.

questions: how are unicode passwords normalized for sasl
subtitle: A preparation profile that rewrites Unicode user names and passwords into one canonical form before they are compared.

tldr.problem: User names and passwords typed by people around the world reach a server as Unicode text, and two spellings of the same name can differ in ways that a byte-by-byte comparison will not notice.
tldr.mechanism: SASLprep is a profile of the stringprep algorithm. It maps some characters, normalizes the result to Unicode normalization form KC, rejects a list of prohibited characters, checks bidirectional strings and lists unassigned code points.
tldr.outcome: The prepared form is canonical, so two spellings that differ only in the ways the profile removes compare equal. The profile was registered in the stringprep profile registry under the name SASLprep.

today: RFC 4013 was a Proposed Standard published in March 2005. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7613, so that document is the current reference for this profile.

sections.title: Why SASLprep Exists
sections.content:
Simple user names and passwords are used pervasively on the Internet for authentication and authorization. People type them with their own keyboards and in their own scripts, so the same account can reach a server as several different sequences of bytes. RFC 4013 defines rules for preparing such strings so that the comparison a server performs matches what a person expected.

For simplicity and implementation ease, a single algorithm is defined for both user names and passwords. The profile is named SASLprep and is a profile of the stringprep algorithm. It is intended for use by Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) mechanisms such as PLAIN, CRAM-MD5 and DIGEST-MD5, and by other protocols that exchange simple user names or passwords.

The profile is not intended for preparing identity strings that are not simple user names, such as email addresses, domain names or distinguished names, and not for strings that require different handling, such as case folding. The algorithm assumes that all strings are made of characters from the Unicode character set.
sections.plainLanguage: SASLprep makes two spellings of the same user name or password become the same string before the server compares them. It is meant for plain user names and passwords, not for email addresses or domain names.

sections.title: The Five Steps of the Profile
sections.content:
The profile builds on stringprep and uses Unicode 3.2. It has five steps.

Mapping. Non-ASCII space characters that can be mapped to SPACE (U+0020) are mapped to it, and the characters that stringprep calls commonly mapped to nothing are mapped to nothing. Normalization. The string is normalized using Unicode normalization form KC, as described in Section 4 of stringprep.

Prohibited output. The profile names the following characters as prohibited input: non-ASCII space characters, ASCII control characters, non-ASCII control characters, private use characters, non-character code points, surrogate code points, characters inappropriate for plain text, characters inappropriate for canonical representation, characters that change display properties or are deprecated, and tagging characters. Bidirectional characters. Bidirectional strings are checked as described in Section 6 of stringprep. Unassigned code points. The stringprep table A.1 is the list of unassigned code points for this profile.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile runs five steps on a string. It maps some characters to other characters or removes them, normalizes what is left, refuses a list of unusable characters, checks the order of right-to-left and left-to-right text, and lists the code points that are not yet assigned.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a table of examples showing how the algorithm transforms character data.

  • I<U+00AD>X becomes IX, because SOFT HYPHEN is mapped to nothing.
  • user stays user, with no transformation.
  • USER stays USER: case is preserved, so it does not match the second example.
  • <U+00AA> becomes a. The output is in form NFKC and the input was in ISO 8859-1.
  • <U+2168> becomes IX. The output is in form NFKC, so it will match the first example.
  • <U+0007> is an error, because the character is prohibited.
  • <U+0627><U+0031> is an error, because it fails the bidirectional check.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that differences in how a name is typed can disappear: a soft hyphen is removed and a Roman numeral becomes letters. Case is kept, so user and USER stay different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The profile is intended to prepare simple user name and password strings for comparison or use in cryptographic functions such as message digests. The preparation algorithm was specifically designed so that its output is canonical and well formed.

The RFC records one known problem. Because of an anomaly in the specification of Unicode normalization, canonical equivalence is not guaranteed for a select few character sequences. Those sequences, however, do not appear in well-formed text. The specification was published despite this known technical problem, and was expected to be revised before it progressed further on the Standards Track, after the Unicode and stringprep specifications were updated to address the problem.

Application of string preparation has an impact on the feasibility of brute force and dictionary attacks. The number of possible prepared strings is less than the number of possible Unicode strings, but the number of usable names and passwords is greater than it would be if only ASCII were used. Eliminating some Unicode code point sequences as possible prepared strings generally makes the canonical output forms practicable and prohibits nonsensical inputs.

User names and passwords should be protected from eavesdropping, and the general stringprep and Unicode security considerations apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Preparation makes the prepared form canonical, so the same text always compares the same way. It slightly shrinks the number of possible passwords an attacker has to guess, but it also allows more names than plain ASCII would. User names and passwords still need protection from anyone listening on the network.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC details the SASLprep profile of the stringprep protocol and states that this profile has been registered in the stringprep profile registry. The registry entry records the name of the profile as SASLprep, the RFC in which the profile is defined as RFC 4013, and the indicator whether or not this is the newest version of the profile as the first version.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile is registered in the stringprep registry under the name SASLprep, and this document is marked as its first version.

viz.caption: THE FIVE STEPS OF THE SASLprep PROFILE

items.title: Mapping
items.text: Non-ASCII spaces become SPACE (U+0020); some characters are mapped to nothing.

items.title: Normalization
items.text: The string is normalized to Unicode normalization form KC.

items.title: Prohibited output
items.text: Control, private use, surrogate, tagging and other listed characters are refused.

items.title: Bidirectional check
items.text: Right-to-left and left-to-right text is checked as stringprep describes.

items.title: Unassigned code points
items.text: The stringprep table A.1 is the list of unassigned code points.

data.title: Input, output and comments
data.code:
#  Input            Output     Comments
1  I<U+00AD>X       IX         SOFT HYPHEN mapped to nothing
2  user             user       no transformation
3  USER             USER       case preserved, will not match #2
4  <U+00AA>         a          output is NFKC, input in ISO 8859-1
5  <U+2168>         IX         output is NFKC, will match #1
6  <U+0007>                    Error - prohibited character
7  <U+0627><U+0031>            Error - bidirectional check
